> The requirement provides a false sense of security.

This ISSUE is providing false sense of "security analysis".


Current requirement:
| # | Description | Level |
| :---: | :--- | :---: |
| **1.2.3** | Verify that output encoding or escaping is used when dynamically building JavaScript content (including JSON), **to avoid changing the message or document structure (to avoid JavaScript and JSON injection)**. | 1 |


Let me write that out again: _to avoid changing the **message or document structure** (to avoid JavaScript and JSON injection)._

Did you read the last part of the requirement? Such as the point and the goal of the requirement?


> ... there are many different contexts in JavaScript each requires different type of encoding, escaping or none at all.

The requirement is about keeping the structure; the context of how it will be used does not matter here (for this there is requirement 3.2.1).


> If needed I can share the real-world examples.

You keep repeating it, and doing so, you show the attitude that ASVS is not based on real-world examples or is something purely theoretical. This is not the case. Also, you are not the "real world representative". But if you want to play that card, it can have a spin as well - ASVS attempts to fix widespread real-world problems. Just the fact that some solution is used somewhere does not mean it is the correct way to do that.


> Misleads developers into skipping serialization, example : let json = '{"name": "' + userInput + '"}'; JSON is a data format , if we use JSON.stringfy or returning via api, escaping is not needed.

There is no mislead here. No one should build JSON that way. And if you do, it is easy to execute JavaScript from that injection, just to point out to incorrect context topic in previous line and the next line. So you are in conflict with your own suggestions or comments.


> The requirement groups JavaScript and JSON together, potentially implying they are equally dangerous, which may confuse developers about their distinct risk profiles (JavaScript’s executable nature vs. JSON’s data-only nature).

JSON is JavaScript, the context matter when it is taken into use. This requirement is about keeping the strcuture.


> The statement oversimplifies a complex, context-dependent problem by suggesting "encoding or escaping" as a one solution, potentially leading developers to overlook context-specific measures like sanitization, validation, or avoiding unsafe APIs.

It makes sense to read, what security goal the requirement solves and then comment based on that. Sanitization and input validation here is more business logic area and for unsafe APIs there is other requirement.


> This requires to improve clarity and accuracy which prevents oversimplified mental model of security that is likely to lead a well-intentioned developer to write vulnerable code.

The requirement intentionally keeps it simple - it just requires people read it and understand why it exists - it is clearly written there.

> Could you please clarify Why does 1.2.3 emphasize ‘escaping and encoding’ but not serialization via JSON.stringify, a safer standard for JSON construction
> When you want to add a piece of JSON to a JS UI, like when you are rendering a React page, it’s a common performance pattern to embed the initial JSON in the template as opposed to XHR/Fetch. Just on the first hit.
> 
> In this situation, JSON.stringify is actually *dangerous* and can lead to XSS/Web page injection. It’s safer to embed JSON on web pages using JS encoding/escaping.
> 
> If you would like I can give you an example that shows *why* JSON.stringify in a webpage is actually dangerous! 🙏🏼

I know the issue you are highlighting, please refer this [CVE-2020-28470](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2020-28470) and this [pull request](https://github.com/scullyio/scully/pull/1182/files#diff-0114de56c4576638839dbae5544c8de9609c33e255680dba7c2e3693ceae63b7L151) of the respective cve fix, and I want to clarify that at no point have I suggested skipping encoding or escaping when using serialization APIs like JSON.stringify.

My original question focused on why **serialization** (using JSON.stringify) is not mentioned in the requirement, when encoding and escaping being mentioned. I advocate that serialization is essential for **safe JSON construction**.

The “common performance pattern” used in SSR frameworks. Every major server-side rendering framework (like Next.js, Nuxt, etc.) follows this safe pattern:

* **Use JSON.stringify() on the server to serialize data,**
* **Then apply context-specific escaping (e.g., for <script> or HTML).** 

Here's an example from Next.js, where they serialize the data with JSON.stringify() and then escape the result to safely embed it in the HTML page.

So as per me:

* **Serialization (JSON.stringify) is essential for [JSON construction](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/canary/packages/next/src/server/render.tsx#L1237)**.
* **Escaping and encoding is required for safe embedding, particularly into script or HTML contexts.Please [refer the specs](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/e2b6a50aec59c42b2c0450a899005d5dbd5cb932/test/unit/htmlescape.test.ts#L4)**

I hope this aligns with your question.

I'm not fully sure I can understand the question, and as we can see - Jim answered also on a bit different direction than (my assumption) it was intended.

JSON libraries, parson the JSON etc, are not in the scope for this requirement and should not be discussed here. The requirement limits itself clearly to "when dynamically building JavaScript content". That also means, when you are serializing for JSON, you don't build dynamically JavaScript content and/or the required encoding and escaping is done when doing so.

If your question is, should a developer manually build a JSON with "string-concat method", then the answer is no, as I already stated in my [initial response](https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/3212#issuecomment-3109561454).

Using a bit different view:
> Are you saying that it is the developer’s responsibility to take care all necessary security measures <whatever comes here>

The answer is: yes, developers are responsible for security.

In case you did not get the expected answer, please rephrase your question. Use code examples if needed.
